components.note: 宀 (roof) — represents a home.
各 (each, various) — a person arriving from elsewhere and welcomed under one's roof gave 客 its meaning 'guest, visitor.'
气 (simplified from 氣) depicts rising wisps or vapor, like breath or steam drifting upward — a simple picture of air or gas.

example.hanzi: 你太客气了,不用送礼物。
example.pinyin: Nǐ tài kèqi le, bú yòng sòng lǐwù.
example.english: You're too polite, no need to bring a gift.
example.fact: 客气 is the polite half of a fixed conversational pair: the standard reply to 谢谢 ("thank you") is 不客气 ("you're welcome", literally "don't be so polite"), and a host telling a guest 别客气 is inviting them to stop being so formal and just relax.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 造's meaning 'to make, build,' an action carried through to completion.
告 (gào) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zào.

example.hanzi: 这场事故造成了严重的交通堵塞。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng shìgù zàochéngle yánzhòng de jiāotōng dǔsè.
example.english: This accident caused severe traffic congestion.
example.fact: 造成 almost always attaches to a negative or neutral consequence — 损失 (loss), 影响 (impact), 堵塞 (congestion) — for a good outcome Chinese reaches instead for 带来 ("to bring") or 产生 ("to produce"), so hearing 造成 primes a listener to expect that something has gone wrong.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 经过三年的努力,他终于成功了。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò sān nián de nǔlì, tā zhōngyú chénggōng le.
example.english: After three years of effort, he finally succeeded.
example.fact: 经过 bridges a literal and a figurative sense with the same verb: passing by a physical place (经过一家商店, "pass by a shop") and passing through a stretch of time or effort (经过三年的努力, "after three years of effort") — one word for both a spatial and a temporal journey.

components.note: 冂 depicts a boundary or border enclosing an area.
土 (earth/land) — the land enclosed within the border.
口 here depicts a well within that land — together giving 周 its early meaning of a bounded territory, and later 'circumference, week, the Zhou dynasty.'
木 (tree) forms the base.
一 marks the very top of the tree, giving 末 its meaning 'end, tip, final.'

example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒmen qù páshān ba.
example.english: Let's go hiking this weekend.
example.fact: 末 pictures the very tip of a tree — 木 (tree) with a stroke marking its topmost point — so 周末 literally names "the tip of the week." The same 末 marks the tail end of other periods too, as in 月末 ("end of the month") and 年末 ("year-end").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 号 relates to calling or crying out aloud, as well as a spoken or marked sign
丂 gives a loose sound connection to 号's reading hào

example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ méiyǒu shǒujī xìnhào.
example.english: There's no cell phone signal here.
example.fact: 信号 spans both the literal (a WiFi or cell signal, a traffic light) and the figurative (释放信号, "to send a signal/hint") — much like English "signal" moves easily between electronics and body language without needing separate words.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跟 originally referred to the heel of the foot, extended to mean 'to follow (on someone's heels)'
艮 (gèn) gives a loose sound connection to 跟's reading gēn
足 (foot) — 踪 names the footprints or tracks left behind.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踪.

example.hanzi: 警察在跟踪那个嫌疑人。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài gēnzōng nàge xiányírén.
example.english: The police are tailing that suspect.
example.fact: Both halves of 跟踪 are built on 足 ("foot"): 跟 originally named the heel — later "to follow on someone's heels" — and 踪 named the footprints left behind, so the compound literally strings together "heel" and "footprint" as two foot-based images for the same act of tracking someone.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喝 describes an action of the mouth, drinking.
曷 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match with 喝.
酉 (a wine jar) — the vessel holding the drink
氵 (liquid) — the wine itself inside the jar

example.hanzi: 他晚上喜欢跟朋友喝酒。
example.pinyin: Tā wǎnshang xǐhuan gēn péngyou hējiǔ.
example.english: He likes drinking with friends in the evening.
example.fact: 喝酒 is the default, unmarked way to say "to drink" in a social context — bare 喝 usually needs an explicit object to be clear (喝水, 喝茶) — so asking a friend "喝了没" ("have you had a drink") is often understood by convention to mean alcohol specifically, even without saying 酒.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 键 originally named a metal bolt or pin, extending to a mechanical 'key.'
建 (jiàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 键.

example.hanzi: 解决问题的关键是找到原因。
example.pinyin: Jiějué wèntí de guānjiàn shì zhǎodào yuányīn.
example.english: The key to solving the problem is finding the cause.
example.fact: 键 originally named a metal bolt or pin that locks a mechanism shut (built on 钅, "metal") — so 关键 literally combines "the bolt (键) that closes a gate (关)", the single pin without which a whole mechanism fails, behind today's abstract sense of "the crucial point."

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
冫 (originally a mark for repetition, unrelated to its later meaning 'ice') — suggests something done more than once.
欠 (a person yawning, mouth open) — repeated yawning gave 次 its meaning of a 'time' or occurrence, as in counting how many times something happens.

example.pinyin: Xiàcì wǒmen zǎodiǎn chūfā.
example.english: Next time let's leave a bit earlier.
example.fact: 次 is Mandarin's measure word for a countable occurrence (一次, 两次, "once, twice"). 下次 substitutes 下 ("next, following") for a number before that same counter, the same pattern behind 上次 ("last time") and 这次 ("this time").

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 满's meaning 'full,' water filling to the brim.
㒼 (mán) gives a sound hint — 满 is pronounced mǎn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Fángjiān lǐ chōngmǎnle xiàoshēng.
example.english: The room was filled with laughter.
example.fact: 充满 almost always takes an abstract or sensory noun as its object — sound, emotion, hope (充满希望) — rather than a countable physical object; "the box is full of apples" reaches instead for 装满, built on 装 ("to pack, load").

example.hanzi: 除了这个,还有其它办法吗?
example.pinyin: Chúle zhège, hái yǒu qítā bànfǎ ma?
example.english: Besides this, are there other ways?
example.fact: 其它 is essentially interchangeable with the far more common 其他 — the only difference is the final character's radical, 它 (originally a snake, generalized to "it" for non-human things) versus 他 (the person radical). Some style guides reserve 其它 for non-human "others" and 其他 for everything, though most writers don't bother with the distinction.

meanings: to put off a discussion until later

components.note: 再 depicts something stacked again on top of a base line — repetition, or doing something 'once more,' is pictured by piling on an extra layer.
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒmen yǐhòu zàishuō.
example.english: Let's talk about this matter later.
example.fact: 再说 does double duty as a literal verb phrase — deferring something to later (以后再说, "we'll talk about it later") — and as a connective at the start of a new clause meaning "moreover, besides" (再说,他也不同意, "besides, he doesn't agree either"). The same two characters cover both a concrete postponement and an abstract argumentative pivot.

meanings: to go to the bottom of a matter
when all is said and done

components.note: 穴 (cave/hole) — 究's meaning 'to explore deeply, investigate' has been linked to exploring a cave.
九 (jiǔ) gives a sound hint — 究 is pronounced jiū, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
音 (music/sound) — a musical piece being performed
儿 (a person) — the performer finishing the piece

example.pinyin: Nǐ jiūjìng xiǎng shuō shénme?
example.english: What exactly are you trying to say?
example.fact: 究竟 intensifies a question, pushing past evasion or confusion toward the real, final answer (你究竟想说什么, "what are you REALLY trying to say") — that insistent, get-to-the-bottom-of-it flavor sets it apart from its closest synonym 到底, though the two are often interchangeable in casual speech.

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.hanzi: 祝你有一个美好的未来。
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ yǒu yígè měihǎo de wèilái.
example.english: I wish you a beautiful future.
example.fact: 美好 is reserved almost exclusively for abstract, positive things — a future, a memory, a wish, a life (美好的回忆, 美好的生活) — and essentially never describes a person's or object's physical appearance, where 漂亮 or 好看 take over instead; mixing the two up is a common learner slip.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恐 describes fear felt in the heart.
巩 (gǒng) gives a sound close to kǒng, sharing the same rhyme.
忄 (heart) — 怕 relates to a feeling of fear in one's heart
白 (bái) gives a loose sound connection to 怕's reading pà

example.pinyin: Kǒngpà tā jīntiān búhuì lái le.
example.english: I'm afraid he won't come today.
example.fact: Although both 恐 and 怕 independently mean "to fear," 恐怕 has grammaticalized into a sentence-opening hedge — "I'm afraid that..." — used to soften bad news or an uncertain guess, much like English "I'm afraid" no longer implies the speaker is actually scared.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 惯 describes a mental pattern, a habit.
贯 (guàn) is an exact match for the sound of 惯.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐjīng xíguànle zǎoqǐ.
example.english: I'm already used to getting up early.
example.fact: 习惯 slides between noun ("a habit," 一个好习惯) and verb ("to be used to," 习惯早起) without changing form at all — a flexibility Chinese allows freely that English marks with two separate words.

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.hanzi: 梦想和现实总是有差距的。
example.pinyin: Mèngxiǎng hé xiànshí zǒngshì yǒu chājù de.
example.english: There's always a gap between dreams and reality.
example.fact: 现实 reuses the same 现 found in 现在 ("now") — built on 见, "to see" — pairing it with 实 ("solid, true") turns "what is now appearing" into "what is solidly true": reality, as opposed to mere appearance or wish.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 做 relates to a person carrying out an action.
故 (cause, reason, to happen) — combined with 亻 (person), 做 came to mean 'to make' or 'to do,' someone actively causing something to happen.
屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ zuòchūle xīn de juédìng.
example.english: The government made a new decision.
example.fact: 做出 rarely stands alone — it habitually pairs with a small set of abstract nouns like 决定 (decision), 贡献 (contribution), or 选择 (choice), functioning closer to "to produce X as a result" than the bare dictionary gloss "to put out, to issue" suggests.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
王 here is a variant of 玉 (jade), appearing once on each side of the character.
刂 (knife) — cutting a piece of jade in two, symbolizing a division into groups, gave 班 its meaning 'class, group.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān bādiǎn shàngbān.
example.english: I go to work at eight every day.
example.fact: 上班 pairs with its neat opposite 下班 ("to get off work") the same way 上车/下车 ("get on/off a vehicle") and 上课/下课 ("start/end class") pair — 上 and 下 ("on" and "off") form one of Mandarin's most productive antonym templates.

components.note: 走 (run/walk) — relates to 越's meaning 'to exceed, cross over,' running past a boundary.
戉 (yuè) gives the sound — 越 is also pronounced yuè, an exact match.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'
走 (run/walk) — relates to 越's meaning 'to exceed, cross over,' running past a boundary.
戉 (yuè) gives the sound — 越 is also pronounced yuè, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tiānqì yuèláiyuè lěng le.
example.english: The weather is getting colder and colder.
example.fact: 越来越 collapses the pattern 越...越... ("the more..., the more...") around the verb 来 ("to come") — literally "increasingly coming to increasingly." It must be followed directly by an adjective or verb (越来越冷, 越来越喜欢), never by a bare noun.

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng jiǎnchá yíxià kèrén míngdān.
example.english: Please check the guest list.
example.fact: 名单 transparently combines 名 ("name") with 单, Mandarin's general word for an itemized sheet — the same 单 behind 菜单 ("menu," a list of dishes) and 账单 ("bill," a list of charges).

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'

example.hanzi: 很不幸,他们的车在路上坏了。
example.pinyin: Hěn búxìng, tāmen de chē zài lùshang huài le.
example.english: Unfortunately, their car broke down on the road.
example.fact: 不幸 is simply 幸 ("lucky, fortunate" — also seen in this batch's 幸福, "happiness") negated by 不, giving Mandarin a tidy fortunate/unfortunate pair. Unlike most 不 + adjective negations, 不幸 has settled into common use as a noun in its own right ("a misfortune"), not just a negated adjective.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 恢 describes a broad, expansive mental capacity, as in 'to restore, magnanimous.'
灰 (huī) gives the sound — an exact match with 恢.
亻 (a person) — the one repeating the routine.
日 (day, sun) — going somewhere every day, a repeated routine giving 复 its meaning 'to repeat, return; again.'

example.pinyin: Tā shēngbìng hòu huīfù de hěn kuài.
example.english: He recovered quickly after being sick.
example.fact: 恢复 covers a wide swath of English's separate verbs "recover, restore, resume" — health (恢复健康), a connection or service (恢复网络), even a past relationship (恢复联系) — letting one Chinese word do the work that English splits across bodies, systems, and situations.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.
讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.

example.pinyin: Qǐng quèrèn nín de hángbān xìnxī.
example.english: Please confirm your flight information.
example.fact: 确 contributes a sense of solidity (built on 石, "stone") and 认 contributes "to recognize, acknowledge" (built on 讠, "speech") — together 确认 literally means to "firmly acknowledge" something, which is why it feels stronger and more deliberate than a bare 认 alone.

components.note: 取 (a hand at an ear) — gathering information or people.
乑 (people standing side by side) — together giving 聚 its meaning 'to assemble, gather.'
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.hanzi: 周末我们有一个同学聚会。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒmen yǒu yígè tóngxué jùhuì.
example.english: We have a classmate gathering this weekend.
example.fact: 聚 alone already means "to assemble" (built from a hand gathering at an ear, plus a cluster of people standing side by side) and 会 separately can mean "to meet" — 聚会 reinforces two near-synonymous "gathering" verbs into one noun, the same synonym-doubling strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该 in the pilot batch.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怀 relates to feelings held close to the heart
不 (bù) gives a sound distantly related to 怀's reading huái, having drifted apart over time
乃 depicts a bent figure, read here as a woman's body.
子 (child) sits beneath — together picturing a woman about to deliver a child, giving 孕 its meaning 'pregnant.'

example.pinyin: Tā huáiyùn sān gè yuè le.
example.english: She's three months pregnant.
example.fact: 怀 carries a sense of "holding close to the heart" (built on 忄, "heart"), while 孕 pictures a body with a child tucked beneath it (乃 over 子) — 怀孕 literally combines "carrying" with "a child within," a fairly transparent image behind the modern medical term.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
囗 (an enclosure) — a garden like 园 is an enclosed area of land.
元 (yuán) gives the sound — an exact match with 园.

example.hanzi: 孩子们喜欢在公园里玩。
example.pinyin: Háizimen xǐhuan zài gōngyuán lǐ wán.
example.english: Children like playing in the park.
example.fact: 园 already means "garden" on its own, as in 花园 ("flower garden") or 果园 ("orchard") — 公园 simply marks that particular garden as "public" (公) rather than private, the same 公 that turns 司 into 公司 ("company," literally a "public office").

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绑 relates to tying something with thread or rope.
邦 (bāng) gives a sound close to bǎng, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.
木 (wood) — racks and frames like 架 were traditionally built of wood.
加 (jiā) gives a rhyme close to jià, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 他被绑架了三天才被救出来。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi bǎngjiàle sān tiān cái bèi jiù chūlái.
example.english: He was kidnapped for three days before being rescued.
example.fact: 绑架 almost always shows up in the passive voice with 被 (被绑架, "to be kidnapped"), since the sentence's focus naturally lands on the victim rather than the kidnapper — a good example of how 被, Mandarin's clearest passive marker, gets reached for almost automatically when something bad happens to someone.

components.note: 阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).
艹 (grass/plant) — 落 relates to leaves or plants falling
洛 (luò) gives the sound — 落 is also pronounced luò, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这个部落有自己的语言和传统。
example.pinyin: Zhège bùluò yǒu zìjǐ de yǔyán hé chuántǒng.
example.english: This tribe has its own language and traditions.
example.fact: 落 (built on 艹, "plant," originally "to fall," as leaves do) extends by association to a settled cluster of dwellings, a "village" — 部落 pairs that settlement sense with 部 ("a division," also seen in 部门, "department") to name a self-contained community: a tribe.

components.note: 贝 (shell/money) — 资 relates to wealth, funds, and resources.
次 (cì) gives a hint of the sound — 资 is pronounced zī, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
米 (rice) — the grain being measured.
斗 (a measuring ladle) — measuring out rice gave 料 its meaning 'material, to estimate, to reckon.'

example.hanzi: 我需要收集一些资料来写报告。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào shōují yìxiē zīliào lái xiě bàogào.
example.english: I need to gather some materials to write the report.
example.fact: 资料 spans a wider range than any single English word — "material" for a report, "data" for research, and in internet slang a user's personal "profile" (个人资料) — one word doing service for physical reference documents and digital identity alike.

components.note: A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'
冫 (water/ice) — 净 relates to washing something clean and pure.
争 (zhēng) is only distantly related in sound to jìng — both end in a nasal final, but the initial and exact rhyme have drifted apart.

example.pinyin: Bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo gānjìng.
example.english: Clean the room thoroughly.
example.fact: 干净 frequently appears as a resultative complement tacked onto a cleaning verb — 打扫干净 ("sweep until clean"), 洗干净 ("wash until clean") — rather than standing alone; Mandarin's verb+result-adjective construction packs "do X until Y is achieved" into one compact phrase.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.
女 (woman) — 姻 describes a relationship formed through marriage.
因 (cause, reason — here 'by virtue of') contributes to the character's form, describing a bond created by marriage.

example.pinyin: Tāmen de hūnyīn hěn xìngfú.
example.english: Their marriage is very happy.
example.fact: Both halves of 婚姻 are built on the 女 ("woman") radical — 婚 historically centered on the bride, and 姻 named the kinship formed through marriage — a small reminder of how the classical vocabulary around marriage was written primarily from the bride's side.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick) — 教 relates to instructing or disciplining, the traditional action of teaching.
孝 (xiào) gives a hint of the sound — 教 is pronounced jiào, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
土 (earth) — 堂 names a hall, a large room built on the ground.
尚 (shàng) gives a rhyme close to táng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 他们在教堂举行了婚礼。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài jiàotáng jǔxíngle hūnlǐ.
example.english: They held their wedding at the church.
example.fact: 教堂 literally means "a hall (堂) for religion/teaching (教)" — the same 教 that gives 教育 ("education") and 宗教 ("religion") is paired here with 堂, the generic word for a large ceremonial hall also seen in 食堂 ("dining hall") and 礼堂 ("auditorium").

components.note: 亻 (person) — 健 describes a person's physical condition.
建 depicts building or constructing — a person strong enough to build things gave 健 its meaning 'strong, healthy.'
广 depicts a simple roofed building, a home.
隶 depicts a servant or laborer — a household with help was traditionally a sign of ease and well-being, giving 康 its meaning 'healthy, peaceful.'

example.pinyin: Duō yùndòng duì jiànkāng yǒu hǎochù.
example.english: Exercising more is good for health.
example.fact: 健康 works as both noun ("health," 关心健康, "care about one's health") and adjective ("healthy," 他很健康, "he is healthy") without changing form — one more case in this deck where a single Chinese word covers what English splits into two.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — represents a home.
各 (each, various) — a person arriving from elsewhere and welcomed under one's roof gave 客 its meaning 'guest, visitor.'
户 (a simplified form of 戶) depicts a single door panel swinging on its hinge.

example.hanzi: 这家公司有很多国外客户。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī yǒu hěnduō guówài kèhù.
example.english: This company has many overseas clients.
example.fact: 客户 is the business-register word for a paying client or account holder — a bank, a law firm, a software company all have 客户 — while a shopper walking into a physical store is more often called 顾客; 客户 leans professional/B2B, 顾客 leans retail/everyday.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 脑 refers to the brain, a part of the body
衣 (clothing) — 袋 names something made of cloth or similar material, a bag.
代 (dài) is an exact match for the sound of 袋.

example.pinyin: Tā bù xiǎoxīn zhuàngdàole nǎodai.
example.english: He accidentally bumped his head.
example.fact: 脑袋 is the casual, colloquial word for "head" — the plainer, more neutral term is simply 头, usable everywhere — much like English has both plain "head" and the more informal "noggin," with 脑袋 pitched at that friendlier, chattier register.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
多 (more/many) — 够 relates to having a sufficient amount
句 (jù) gives a loose sound connection to 够's reading gòu

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē qián búgòu mǎi jīpiào.
example.english: This money isn't enough to buy a plane ticket.
example.fact: 不够 can modify a noun directly (钱不够, "[the] money [is] not enough") or an adjective to mean "not X enough" (不够好, "not good enough") — the same negated 够 covers both a quantity shortfall and a quality shortfall, two ideas English keeps grammatically apart.

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.pinyin: Qiánmiàn yǒu yígè hónglǜdēng.
example.english: There's a traffic light ahead.
example.fact: 前面 pairs with 后面 ("behind") the way 上面/下面 pair for "above/below" — 面 ("face, surface, side") is Mandarin's default suffix for turning a bare directional word into a locatable place, the building block behind a whole family: 前面, 后面, 里面, 外面.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.pinyin: Tāmen shàng gè yuè fēnshǒu le.
example.english: They broke up last month.
example.fact: 分手 literally means "to divide (分) hands (手)" — unclasping joined hands as a physical image for parting ways, whether between traveling companions heading off in different directions or, in its most common modern use, a couple ending a relationship.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zǒucuò fāngxiàng le.
example.english: We went the wrong direction.
example.fact: 方向 moves easily from the literal — which way to walk or drive, 问方向 ("ask for directions") — to the figurative, as in a life or career's general direction (人生方向) — much like English "direction" itself bridges the physical and the metaphorical without needing a separate word for either.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā qù kàn xīnlǐ yīshēng le.
example.english: He went to see a psychologist.
example.fact: 心理 (xīnlǐ, "psychology/mentality") is easy to mix up with the near-homophone 心里 (xīnli, "inside one's heart, in one's thoughts") — swapping 理 ("reason, logic") for 里 ("inside") turns a clinical or academic noun into an everyday phrase for private feelings, a mix-up that shows up even in native speakers' typos.

components.note: The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'
礻 (spirit/altar) — 福 relates to blessings granted by the spirits
畐 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 福's reading fú

example.pinyin: Zhù nǐmen xìngfú měimǎn.
example.english: Wishing you happiness and fulfillment.
example.fact: 幸福 describes a deep, lasting sense of well-being and contentment — often tied to family, marriage, or life circumstances — setting it apart from the lighter, more momentary 高兴 or 开心 ("happy, glad" in the moment); saying 祝你幸福 at a wedding carries far more weight than a casual 祝你开心.

components.note: 攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.
令 (an order, command) — 命 pictures issuing a command.
口 (mouth) — a command given aloud gave 命 its meaning 'order' or 'decree,' and by extension, 'fate' or 'life.'

example.pinyin: “Jiùmìng!” tā dàshēng hǎndào.
example.english: "Help!" she shouted loudly.
example.fact: As a stand-alone interjection, 救命! functions like English "Help!" in an emergency, but unlike "help," which can request any kind of assistance, 救命 literally invokes life-or-death stakes ("save my life") — so it's reserved for genuine danger rather than an everyday request for a hand.

meanings: to go on to do sth

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 先吃饭,接着我们去看电影。
example.pinyin: Xiān chīfàn, jiēzhe wǒmen qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: First let's eat, then we'll go watch a movie.
example.fact: As a connective opening a new clause, 接着 sequences events one after another ("and then, next") — distinct from the literal verb sense of 接 alone, "to catch" (接球, "catch a ball"), where here 着 works as a grammatical suffix rather than contributing a separate meaning of its own.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) shows 疯 describes an afflicted state of mind.
风 (fēng) gives the exact sound of 疯.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Bié lǐ tā, tā shì gè fēngzi.
example.english: Don't pay attention to him, he's a lunatic.
example.fact: 疯子 is a blunt, often insulting way to call someone "crazy" — for a softer or more clinical way to talk about mental illness, Chinese instead reaches for 精神病 (a mental disorder) or the plain adjective 疯 alone (他疯了, "he's gone crazy"), which describes a temporary state rather than labeling the person.

meanings: to put sb on the spot

components.note: 丬 (a stylized bed) — 将 originally pictured someone preparing for bed at night.
夕 (evening/night) — the coming of night was seen as predictable, giving 将 its meaning 'about to' or 'going to' happen.
冖 here is a distorted form of 力 (strength) — a simplified way of showing soldiers grouped together.
车 (cart/vehicle) — 军 originally pictured soldiers riding out to battle in war chariots.

example.hanzi: 这位将军带领军队赢得了战争。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi jiāngjūn dàilǐng jūnduì yíngdéle zhànzhēng.
example.english: This general led the army to win the war.
example.fact: Beyond the literal military rank, 将军 doubles as the Chinese-chess (xiangqi) term for "check" — calling out 将军! when directly threatening the opponent's general piece — and by extension the phrase is used figuratively outside the game to mean cornering someone or putting them on the spot, similar to how English "checkmate" became a metaphor beyond the chessboard.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — relates to 技's meaning 'skill, technique,' a skill performed with the hands.
支 (zhī) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jì.

example.hanzi: 这家公司在人工智能技术方面很领先。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī zài réngōng zhìnéng jìshù fāngmiàn hěn lǐngxiān.
example.english: This company is a leader in AI technology.
example.fact: 术 alone broadly means "art, skill, technique" and shows up across many domains — 艺术 ("art"), 手术 ("surgery," literally "hand technique"), 武术 ("martial arts") — with 技术 narrowing that general root specifically toward technical or engineering know-how.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吃 relates to eating, done with the mouth
乞 (qǐ) gives a sound close to 吃's reading chī
饣 (food) — 饭 names cooked rice, a meal.
反 (fǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 饭.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen jǐdiǎn chīfàn?
example.english: What time are we eating?
example.fact: 吃饭 literally means "to eat rice," yet it's used nationwide as the generic "to eat a meal" even in northern China, where wheat noodles and bread are the actual staple — a case where a word's literal ingredient outlived its literal accuracy. It also extends idiomatically to "make a living" (靠什么吃饭, literally "what do you rely on to eat rice").

components.note: 囗 depicts an enclosure or fence.
木 (tree) — a tree hemmed in by a fence, unable to grow freely, gave 困 its meaning 'trapped, difficult.'
又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'

example.pinyin: Kèfú kùnnan xūyào yǒngqì.
example.english: Overcoming difficulties requires courage.
example.fact: 困难 functions as both adjective ("difficult," 这很困难) and noun ("a difficulty/hardship," 遇到困难, "encounter difficulties") — and unlike many two-character adjectives, it can be directly counted with 个 (一个困难, "one difficulty") once used as a noun, treating an abstract hardship almost like a countable object.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
讠 (speech) — 许 relates to giving permission through words.
午 (wǔ) gives a hint of the sound — 许 is pronounced xǔ, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 妈妈不许我看电视到很晚。
example.pinyin: Māma bùxǔ wǒ kàn diànshì dào hěn wǎn.
example.english: Mom doesn't allow me to watch TV until very late.
example.fact: 不许 carries a sharper, more authoritative edge than the neutral 不能 ("cannot, may not") — it's the word a parent, teacher, or rule invokes to flatly forbid something (不许说话! "No talking!"), closer in force to a command than to a simple statement of impossibility.
